claims.source: Such factors—including the absolute reward magnitude of a prospect (Pratt, 1964), the riskiness of a prospect (Weber et al., 2004), or even the sum of the normalised reward and probability (Rouault et al., 2019; Stewart, 2011; Farashahi et al., 2019)—can perturb people's valuations of risky prospects in ways that the expected-value framework does not capture (Peterson et al., 2021). We reasoned that if such factors covaried with the EV of the distractor, then the distractor effects reported previously could, partially or fully, afford alternative interpretations.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on known factors that influence decision-making, supported by citations.

claims.claim: All previous studies reporting positive and interacting distractor effects used the exact same set of trials for all participants.
claims.source: However, we note that all previous studies reporting positive and interacting distractor effects (Chau et al., 2014; Chau et al., 2020) used the exact same set of trials for all participants.
claims.evidence: This is a factual observation about the methodology of previous studies.

claims.claim: The set of trials in previous studies was generated pseudo-randomly, by resampling choice-sets until the EV of the distractor was sufficiently decorrelated from the EV difference between the two targets.
claims.source: This set of trials was generated pseudo-randomly, by resampling choice-sets until the EV of the distractor was sufficiently decorrelated from the EV difference (choice difficulty) between the two targets.
claims.evidence: This describes the trial generation procedure used in previous studies.

claims.claim: Using a single set of trials in conjunction with the decorrelation approach increases the risk of introducing unintended confounding covariations in the elected set of trials.
claims.source: On the negative side, using a single set of trials in conjunction with this decorrelation approach, increases the risk of introducing unintended confounding covariations in the elected set of trials, which in turn will have consistent impact on the group-level behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the potential consequences of the methodology used in previous studies.

claims.claim: If people valuate prospects by simply adding up their payoff and probability information (additive utility), two target prospects with the same EV difference but different additive utility differences will be differently discriminable.
claims.source: For instance, if people valuate prospects by simply adding up their payoff and probability information (hereafter additive utility or AU) (Rouault et al., 2019; Farashahi et al., 2019; Bongioanni et al., 2021), two target prospects both offering £1 with probability of 0.9 vs. 0.8, respectively (i.e., EV difference: 0.1, AU difference: 0.1), will be less easily discriminable than two other prospects both offering £0.5 with probability of 0.5 vs. 0.3, respectively (i.e., EV difference: 0.1, AU difference: 0.2; Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothetical scenario illustrating how additive utility could affect discriminability, with citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: If choice-sets with different AU differences are more frequently associated with different EV distractors, then a positive distractor effect could be attributable to additive integration rather than the distractor's EV.
claims.source: Crucially, if the first choice-set (AU difference: 0.1) is more frequently associated with low-EV distractors than the second one (AU difference: 0.2), then a positive distractor effect could be attributable to additive integration rather than the distractor's EV (Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about how confounding covariations could explain the positive distractor effect.

claims.claim: The EV of the distractor alternative could covary with its relative position in the reward-probability space, which would influence decision accuracy because the relative position of a decoy alternative in the multiattribute choice space can induce strong choice biases.
claims.source: Second, the EV of the distractor alternative could covary with its relative position in the reward-probability space (we call these distractor-related covariations). This would influence decision accuracy because, as outlined earlier, the relative position of a decoy alternative in the multiattribute choice space can induce strong choice biases (Tsetsos et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on known effects of decoy position, supported by citations.

claims.claim: If distractors with high EVs happen to appear closer to the correct target, a positive distractor effect could be entirely attributable to the attraction effect.
claims.source: Under this assumption, if distractors with high EVs happen to appear closer to the correct target (i.e., the target with the highest EV), a positive distractor effect could be entirely attributable to the attraction effect.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothetical scenario illustrating how the attraction effect could explain the positive distractor effect.

claims.claim: The first class of target-related covariations is present in the examined datasets, with positive and interacting 'notional' distractor effects being evident even in matched binary trials, in which the distractor alternative was not present.
claims.source: We began with establishing that the first class of target-related covariations is indeed present in the examined datasets, with positive and interacting 'notional' distractor effects being evident even in matched binary trials, in which the distractor alternative was not present.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on data analysis.

claims.claim: Using a novel baselining approach, distractor effects are eradicated when the influence of unintended covariations is controlled for.
claims.source: Using a novel baselining approach, we asked if there are residual distractor effects when the influence of these unintended covariations is controlled for, reporting that distractor effects are eradicated.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on data analysis.

claims.claim: The target-related confounding covariations are pinpointed to people's strong propensity to integrate reward and probability additively, and not multiplicatively.
claims.source: We then pinpointed these target-related confounding covariations to people's strong propensity to integrate reward and probability additively, and not multiplicatively.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on data analysis and modeling.

claims.claim: Defining the key target and distractor utility variables using subjective (additive) utility revealed a modest negative distractor effect.
claims.source: Moving forward, defining the key target and distractor utility variables, not using EV, but subjective (additive) utility, revealed a modest negative distractor effect.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on data analysis.

claims.claim: Choice accuracy was lawfully influenced by the position of the distractor in the multiattribute space, consistent with a large body of empirical work in multiattribute choice.
claims.source: Moving on to the second class of distractor-related covariations, we established that choice accuracy was lawfully influenced by the position of the distractor in the multiattribute space (Figure 1d), consistent with a large body of empirical work in multiattribute choice (Dumbalska et al., 2020; Tsetsos et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: The 'decoy' influence was most pronounced when the distractor alternative was close to the high-EV (correct) target in the multiattribute space, yielding an attraction effect when the distractor was inferior, and a repulsion effect when the distractor was superior to the target.
claims.source: This 'decoy' influence was most pronounced when the distractor alternative was close to the high-EV (correct) target in the multiattribute space, yielding an attraction effect (i.e., a boost in accuracy) when the distractor was inferior, and a repulsion effect (i.e., a reduction in accuracy) when the distractor was superior (in subjective utility) to the target.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study based on data analysis.

claims.claim: The decoy influence peaking around the high-EV target essentially re-describes a negative distractor effect without evoking ad hoc 'unidimensional distractor' mechanisms other than those that are needed to produce classic multiattribute context effects.
claims.source: Of note, this decoy influence peaking around the high-EV target, essentially re-describes a negative distractor effect without evoking ad hoc 'unidimensional distractor' mechanisms other than those that are needed to produce classic multiattribute context effects (Tsetsos et al., 2010; Tsetsos et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, suggesting a parsimonious explanation.

claims.claim: When confounding covariations are controlled for, only a modest negative distractor effect survives.
claims.source: Overall, our analyses update the state-of-the-art by suggesting that, when confounding covariations are controlled for, only a modest negative distractor effect survives.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the current study.

claims.claim: It is conceivable that the modest negative distractor effect mirrors asymmetric classic multiattribute context effects, which occurred robustly in the examined datasets.
claims.source: Further, it is conceivable that this distractor effect mirrors asymmetric classic multiattribute context effects, which occurred robustly in the examined datasets.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Five datasets from published studies (N = 144 human participants) of a speeded multiattribute decision-making task were re-analysed.
claims.source: We re-analysed five datasets from published studies (Chau et al., 2014; Gluth et al., 2018; N = 144 human participants) of a speeded multiattribute decision-making task.
claims.evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claims.claim: Participants were shown choice alternatives that varied along two distinct reward attributes: reward magnitude (X) and reward probability (P), which mapped to visual features.
claims.source: Participants were shown choice alternatives that varied along two distinct reward attributes: reward magnitude (X) and reward probability (P), which mapped to visual features (colourful slanted bars as options in Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the task.

claims.claim: Participants were instructed to choose the most valuable one among multiple options and to maximise the total reward across trials.
claims.source: After learning the feature-to-attribute mapping, participants were instructed to choose the most valuable one among multiple options placed in this multiattribute space (Figure 2a) on each trial and to maximise the total reward across trials.
claims.evidence: This describes the task instructions given to participants.

claims.claim: In the ternary-choice condition, one option (the 'distractor', or D) was flagged unavailable for selection early in the trial.
claims.source: In the ternary-choice condition, one option (the 'distractor', or D) was flagged unavailable for selection early in the trial.
claims.evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Rational choice theory posits that an unavailable D should not in any way alter the relative choice between two available H and L targets.
claims.source: Rational choice theory posits that an unavailable D should not in any way alter the relative choice between two available H and L targets.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of a principle from rational choice theory.

claims.claim: The behavioural data in the task challenged the view that an unavailable D should not alter the relative choice between two available H and L targets.
claims.source: However, the behavioural data in this task (Chau et al., 2014) challenged this view.
claims.evidence: This references findings from a previous study.

claims.claim: Chau et al., 2014; Chau et al., 2020 reported that a relative distractor variable 'DV − HV' altered relative accuracy.
claims.source: By examining the probability of H being chosen over L in ternary trials, that is, the relative choice accuracy, Chau et al., 2014; Chau et al., 2020 reported that a relative distractor variable 'DV − HV' (the EV difference between the distractor and the best available target) altered relative accuracy.
claims.evidence: This references findings from previous studies.

claims.claim: Other recent studies quantified the distractor influence by means of an absolute distractor variable DV.
claims.source: We note that other recent studies, using different stimuli, quantified the distractor influence by means of an absolute distractor variable DV (Louie et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This references methodological approaches used in other studies.

claims.claim: Participants encountered 'matched' binary trials in which only the H and L target alternatives were shown, in addition to ternary trials in which D was present but unavailable.
claims.source: To begin with, we note that, in addition to ternary trials in which D was present (but unavailable), participants encountered 'matched' binary trials in which only the H and L target alternatives were shown.
claims.evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Binary trials are ideally suited for assessing the extent to which previously reported distractor affects can be attributed to covariations between the distractor variable and target-related properties.
claims.source: These binary trials are ideally suited for assessing the extent to which previously reported distractor affects can be attributed to covariations between the distractor variable and target-related properties.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological insight about the utility of binary trials.

claims.claim: For each ternary trial, a respective binary-choice baseline accuracy can be derived from binary trials that had the exact same targets but no distractor.
claims.source: This is because, for each ternary trial, we can derive a respective binary-choice baseline accuracy from binary trials that had the exact same targets but no distractor (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This describes the baselining approach used in the study.

claims.claim: Given that participants never saw D in binary trials, the distractor variable is notional and should have no effect on the binary baseline accuracies.
claims.source: Given that participants never saw D in binary trials, the distractor variable is notional and should have no effect on the binary baseline accuracies.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about what should be expected in binary trials.

claims.claim: If D paradoxically 'influences' binary accuracies, then this would signal that the distractor variable covaries with other unspecified modulators of choice accuracy.
claims.source: However, if D does paradoxically 'influence' binary accuracies, then this would signal that the distractor variable covaries with other unspecified modulators of choice accuracy.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about what a notional distractor effect would indicate.

claims.claim: A notional distractor effect is not a genuine empirical phenomenon but a tool to diagnose target-related covariations in the experimental design.
claims.source: We emphasise here that a notional distractor effect is not a genuine empirical phenomenon but a tool to diagnose target-related covariations in the experimental design.
claims.evidence: This clarifies the conceptual status of the notional distractor effect.

claims.claim: For the ternary-choice condition, the GLM reveals a significant main effect of the relative distractor variable 'DV − HV' (t(143) = 3.89, p < 0.001), and a significant interaction between this distractor variable and the index of decision difficulty 'HV − LV' on relative choice accuracy, t(143) = −3.67, p < 0.001.
claims.source: For the ternary-choice condition, our GLM reveals a significant main effect of the relative distractor variable 'DV − HV' (t(143) = 3.89, p < 0.001), and a significant interaction between this distractor variable and the index of decision difficulty 'HV − LV' on relative choice accuracy, t(143) = −3.67, p < 0.001 (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the GLM analysis.

claims.claim: The GLM results for ternary choice agree with previous reports when analysing ternary choice alone.
claims.source: These results agree with previous reports when analysing ternary choice alone (Chau et al., 2014; Chau et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This compares the current findings to previous studies.

claims.claim: For matched binary baseline accuracies, the GLM coefficients bear a striking resemblance to those of the ternary-choice GLM, with notional positive and interacting distractor effects being observed.
claims.source: Turning into the matched binary baseline accuracies, the GLM coefficients bear a striking resemblance to those of the ternary-choice GLM (see Figure 2e; also compare Figure 2b to Figure 2c for a stark resemblance between T and B accuracy patterns), with (this time) notional positive and interacting distractor effects being observed.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from the GLM analysis comparing ternary and binary trials.

claims.claim: Neither the main distractor nor the (HV − LV) × (DV – HV) interaction effects are modulated by 'Condition' in a GLM combining T and B together, |t(143)| < 0.92, p > 0.72.
claims.source: Crucially, neither the main distractor nor the (HV − LV) × (DV – HV) interaction effects are modulated by 'Condition' in a GLM combining T and B together, |t(143)| < 0.92, p > 0.72 (Figure 2f).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the GLM analysis.

claims.claim: Similar results are seen when the relative distractor variable DV − HV is replaced by the absolute distractor variable DV or when a covariate HV + LV is additionally included: the distractor's EV had no differential effect on relative accuracy across binary vs. ternary condition.
claims.source: We see similar results when the relative distractor variable DV − HV is replaced by the absolute distractor variable DV or when a covariate HV + LV is additionally included: the distractor's EV had no differential effect on relative accuracy across binary vs. ternary condition (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This reports robustness checks of the main finding.

claims.claim: The notional distractor effects in binary trials indicate that the value of D covaries with target-related properties (other than HV − LV) that modulate choice accuracy.
claims.source: Specifically, the notional distractor effects (Figure 2e) in binary trials (with only H and L stimuli present) indicate that the value of D covaries with target-related properties (other than HV − LV, which was already a regressor) that modulate choice accuracy.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the notional distractor effects.

claims.claim: The original study reported a surprising phenomenon: decisions seem to be particularly vulnerable to disruption by a third low value, as opposed to high value, distracting alternative, that is, a positive distractor effect.
claims.source: The original study reported a surprising phenomenon (Chau et al., 2014): decisions seem to be particularly vulnerable to disruption by a third low value, as opposed to high value, distracting alternative, that is, a positive distractor effect.
claims.evidence: This references a finding from a previous study.

claims.claim: The very definition of the positive distractor effect hinges upon the a priori assumption that decisions rely on calculating and subsequently comparing the EVs across choice options.
claims.source: The very definition of this effect hinges upon the a priori assumption that decisions rely on calculating and subsequently comparing the EVs across choice options.
claims.evidence: This is a critical observation about the assumptions underlying the positive distractor effect.

claims.claim: An alternative prominent idea is that participants eschew EV calculations; instead, they compute the difference between alternatives within each attribute and simply sum up these differences across attributes.
claims.source: An alternative prominent idea is that participants eschew EV calculations (Hayden and Niv, 2021); instead, they compute the difference between alternatives within each attribute and simply sum up these differences across attributes.
claims.evidence: This references an alternative theoretical perspective, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Past studies in binary risky choice have reported decision rules in humans and other animals based on a weighted sum of the attribute differences, that is, a decision variable equivalent to the AU difference between alternatives.
claims.source: Indeed, past studies in binary risky choice have reported decision rules in humans and other animals (Rouault et al., 2019; Farashahi et al., 2019; Bongioanni et al., 2021) based on a weighted sum of the attribute differences, that is, a decision variable equivalent to the AU difference between alternatives, Δ(AU) = λ(HX − LX) + (1 − λ)(HP − LP), where 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1.
claims.evidence: This references findings from previous studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The additive combination of reward and probability may not be generalisable in all types of risky-choice tasks, but it could viably govern decisions in the simple task illustrated in Figure 2a.
claims.source: Although the additive combination of reward and probability may not be generalisable in all types of risky-choice tasks, it could viably govern decisions in the simple task illustrated in Figure 2a.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the applicability of additive utility.

claims.claim: The key distractor variable DV − HV positively covaries with the Δ(AU) between H and L across all choice-sets (e.g., Pearson's r(148) = 0.314, p < 0.0001, in the case of equal weighting between X and P, λ = 0.5).
claims.source: Of note, we came to notice that the key distractor variable DV − HV positively covaries with the Δ(AU) between H and L across all choice-sets (e.g., Pearson's r(148) = 0.314, p < 0.0001, in the case of equal weighting between X and P, λ = 0.5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding about the covariation between variables.

claims.claim: This unintended covariation arose in the original study possibly due to a deliberate attempt to decorrelate two EV-based quantities (DV − HV and HV − LV) in the stimuli.
claims.source: This unintended covariation arose in the original study possibly due to a deliberate attempt to decorrelate two EV-based quantities (DV − HV and HV − LV) in the stimuli (Chau et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed covariation.

claims.claim: The correlation between DV − HV and Δ(AU) is stronger in more difficult trials (r(71) = 0.52, p < 0.0001, shared variance = 27%) than in easier trials (r(59) = 0.43, p < 0.001, shared variance = 19%), mirroring both the positive and the interacting notional distractor effects on binary choice.
claims.source: The correlation between DV − HV and Δ(AU) is stronger in more difficult trials (r(71) = 0.52, p < 0.0001, shared variance = 27%; splitting 150 trials into difficult vs. easy by the median of HV − LV; Chau et al., 2020) than in easier trials (r(59) = 0.43, p < 0.001, shared variance = 19%), mirroring both the positive (overall positive correlation) and the interacting (change of correlation strength as a function of difficulty) notional distractor effects on binary choice.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding about the covariation between variables as a function of difficulty.

claims.claim: DV − HV negatively covaries with HV + LV (Pearson's r(148) = −0.78, p < 0.001), which potentially leads to another explanation of why binary-choice accuracy seems lower as the matched DV − HV variable decreases.
claims.source: Notably, DV − HV also negatively covaries with HV + LV (Pearson's r(148) = −0.78, p < 0.001), which potentially leads to another explanation of why binary-choice accuracy seems lower as the matched DV − HV variable decreases.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding about the covariation between variables.

claims.claim: This explanation appeals to the divisive normalisation (DN) model based on EV.
claims.source: This explanation appeals to the divisive normalisation (DN) model based on EV (Louie et al., 2013; Pirrone et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This references a theoretical model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: DN applied to EVs will shrink the EV difference between H and L more aggressively for choice-sets with larger HV + LV, rendering them harder choice problems (lower accuracy).
claims.source: DN applied to EVs ('EV + DN', hereafter) will shrink the EV difference between H and L more aggressively for set 2 than for set 1 because of the larger denominator in set 2, rendering set 2 a harder choice problem (lower accuracy).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the predictions of the DN model.

claims.claim: Adding the HV + LV covariate to the GLMs does not explain away the interacting notional distractor effects in binary trials.
claims.source: It is important to note that, in line with previous analyses (Chau et al., 2014; Gluth et al., 2018), adding the HV + LV covariate to the GLMs does not explain away the interacting notional distractor effects in binary trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the GLM analysis.

claims.claim: The 'AU' and 'EV + DN' hypotheses both predict a positive main notional distractor effect on binary-choice accuracy, but their predictions for the (HV − LV) × (DV − HV) interaction could differ.
claims.source: Qualitatively, the above two hypotheses ('AU' vs. 'EV + DN') both predict a positive main notional distractor effect on binary-choice accuracy, but their predictions for the (HV − LV) × (DV − HV) interaction could differ.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the predictions of two theoretical models.

claims.claim: DN might even predict a slightly positive, rather than negative, interacting notional distractor effect on binary accuracy—in this stimulus set, the divisively normalised Δ(EV) happens to be more positively correlated with DV − HV in easier trials (shared variance = 39.8%) than in harder trials (shared variance = 36.7%).
claims.source: For instance, DN might even predict a slightly positive, rather than negative, interacting notional distractor effect on binary accuracy—in this stimulus set, the divisively normalised Δ(EV) happens to be more positively correlated with DV − HV in easier trials (shared variance = 39.8%) than in harder trials (shared variance = 36.7%).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding about the predictions of the DN model in this specific stimulus set.

claims.claim: AU on its own can approximate the EV sum effect by nearly tripling the utility difference between H and L in set 1 compared with that in set 2, which also renders set 2 more difficult.
claims.source: It is also important to note that AU on its own can approximate this EV sum effect by nearly tripling the utility difference between H and L in set 1 compared with that in set 2, which also renders set 2 more difficult (Figure 2g, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about how AU can mimic the EV sum effect.

claims.claim: Both the EV + DN model and the AU model (with a free λ parameter; mean λ estimate: 0.46, SE: 0.017) predict a positive 'notional distractor' main effect on binary accuracy.
claims.source: As expected, both the EV + DN model and the AU model (with a free λ parameter; mean λ estimate: 0.46, SE: 0.017) predict a positive 'notional distractor' main effect on binary accuracy (Figure 2h, i).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The AU model, but not the EV + DN model, reproduces a negative notional (HV − LV) × (DV − HV) interaction effect on accuracy, mirroring the human data.
claims.source: However, the AU model, but not the EV + DN model, reproduces a negative notional (HV − LV) × (DV − HV) interaction effect on accuracy (Figure 2i), mirroring the human data (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling comparing model predictions to human data.

claims.claim: The AU model qualitatively provides a parsimonious account of why notional distractor effects occurred in binary trials.
claims.source: The AU model thus qualitatively provides a parsimonious account of why notional distractor effects occurred in binary trials.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claims.claim: The naive EV model fundamentally deviates from the human choice data: the model predicts a vertical gradient of choice accuracy constrained by HV − LV.
claims.source: Qualitatively, Figure 3a shows that the naive EV model fundamentally deviates from the human choice data: the model predicts a vertical gradient of choice accuracy constrained by HV − LV.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling comparing model predictions to human data.

claims.claim: When comparing models head-to-head using a cross-validation scheme, the AU model wins over any other model (protected exceedance probability Ppexc > 0.99).
claims.source: When comparing these models head-to-head using a cross-validation scheme, we find that the AU model wins over any other model (Figure 3b; protected exceedance probability Ppexc > 0.99; Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian model comparison.

claims.claim: The AU model's superiority holds robustly when including, in all models, subjective non-linear distortions of attributes.
claims.source: This result still holds robustly when including, in all models, subjective non-linear distortions of attributes (Zhang and Maloney, 2012; 'Non-linear' in Figure 3b, c right panels; Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian model comparison with additional model variants.

claims.claim: The RTs predicted by the DN model mismatch the human RTs.
claims.source: Moreover, the RTs predicted by the DN model mismatch the human RTs (Figure 3a: 'EV + DN').
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling comparing model predictions to human data.

claims.claim: DN still fails to win over the AU model even when considering static versions of the models fitted to the choice probabilities alone while ignoring the RTs.
claims.source: DN still fails to win over the AU model even when we consider static versions of the models fitted to the choice probabilities alone while ignoring the RTs (Figure 3c, 'Static models'; Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian model comparison with static model variants.

claims.claim: The AU model is favoured over specific and popular instantiations of the non-linear multiplicative model (i.e., expected utility and prospect theory).
claims.source: Additional model comparisons corroborate that the AU model is favoured over specific and popular instantiations of the non-linear multiplicative model (i.e., expected utility [Von Neumann and Morgenstern, 2007] and prospect theory [Kahneman and Tversky, 1979]; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian model comparison.

claims.claim: The success of the AU model suggests that the reward attributes were not multiplicatively conglomerated into a single EV dimension.
claims.source: The success of the AU model suggests that the reward attributes were not multiplicatively conglomerated into a single EV dimension.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claims.claim: The EV model, being only sensitive to the difference in the product of probability and reward, fails to capture any performance variations across condition categories (single dom. vs. double dom.).
claims.source: The EV model, being only sensitive to the difference in the product of probability and reward, fails to capture any performance variations across these distinct categories (because these categories are orthogonal to the EV difference; Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling comparing model predictions to human data.

claims.claim: The AU model can capture performance variations across condition categories (single dom. vs. double dom.).
claims.source: By contrast, the AU model can capture these across-category performance changes (Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling comparing model predictions to human data.

claims.claim: The dual-route model's deviation from human behaviour becomes more salient when inspecting the model predictions at each fixed level of EV difference.
claims.source: Qualitatively, the dual-route model seems to be able to capture some patterns of the human data on the binned maps (Figure 3a: 'Dual-route'), but its deviation from human behaviour becomes more salient when we inspect the model predictions at each fixed level of EV difference (Figure 3f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling comparing model predictions to human data.

claims.claim: The AU model reproduces the patterns of both accuracy and RT in binary-choice trials decisively better than the models relying on EV or divisively normalised EV.
claims.source: Taken together, we show that the AU model reproduces the patterns of both accuracy and RT in binary-choice trials decisively better than the models relying on EV or divisively normalised EV (also see Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2 for model parameter estimates).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results.

claims.claim: The dynamic AU model was fit to binary and ternary choices separately, and subjective utility was constructed as AU = λ(X) + (1 − λ)(P).
claims.source: To better define these variables, we fit the dynamic AU model (with free λ weight; Methods: Context-independent model) to binary and ternary choices, separately, and constructed subjective utility as AU = λ(X) + (1 − λ)(P).
claims.evidence: This describes the modeling approach used.

claims.claim: A significant negative main distractor effect, AUD × C, on the choice accuracy was found, t(143) = −2.27, p = 0.024 (uncorrected).
claims.source: We found a significant negative main distractor effect, AUD × C, on the choice accuracy, t(143) = −2.27, p = 0.024 (uncorrected)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the GLM analysis.

claims.claim: The main distractor effect was marginally significant when using the relative distractor variable AUD – AUH, t(143) = −1.86, p = 0.065 (uncorrected).
claims.source: however, this main effect was marginally significant when using the relative distractor variable AUD – AUH, t(143) = −1.86, p = 0.065 (uncorrected).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the GLM analysis.

claims.claim: The interacting distractor effect was not significant, t(143) < −0.54, p > 0.1.
claims.source: The interacting distractor effect was not significant t(143) < −0.54, p > 0.1 (see Supplementary file 3 for a full report).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the GLM analysis.

claims.claim: By contrast, neither the main nor the interacting distractor effects were significant in the GLM with EV-based regressors (p > 0.3, uncorrected).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the GLM analysis.

claims.claim: The results based on subjective AU fit more closely with recent reports showing a negative main distractor effect.

claims.evidence: This compares the current findings to previous studies.

claims.claim: 84% of the ternary trials satisfy specific H, L, and D geometric configurations that could give rise to attraction and repulsion effects.

claims.evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the stimulus set.

claims.claim: An attraction effect occurs whereby the probability of choosing a target over a competitor increases due to the presence of an 'inferior' dominated D near the target.
claims.source: First, an attraction effect (Huber et al., 1982), whereby the probability of choosing a target over a competitor increases due to the presence of an 'inferior' dominated D near the target (also see Figure 1d for an illustrative example)

claims.claim: A repulsion effect occurs whereby the pattern is reversed (and the probability of choosing the target is reduced) in the presence of a nearby 'superior' dominating D.
claims.source: and second, a repulsion effect (Dumbalska et al., 2020), whereby this pattern is reversed (and the probability of choosing the target is reduced) in the presence of a nearby 'superior' dominating D.
claims.evidence: This describes a known effect in decision-making research, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Other popular context effects, such as the similarity and the compromise effects, could not be examined here due to the absence or the very low frequency of occurrence of appropriate choice-sets.
claims.source: We note in passing that other popular context effects, such as the similarity and the compromise effects, could not be examined here due to the absence or the very low frequency of occurrence of appropriate choice-sets (i.e., in these effects the decoys are required to be roughly iso-preferable to the target or the competitor alternatives, Spektor et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological note about the limitations of the stimulus set.

claims.claim: A condition-unspecific change in behaviour, that is, an accuracy reduction potentially induced by higher cognitive demands in the ternary trials, was considered.
claims.source: Before characterising decoy effects, we considered the possibility that the change of relative accuracy between binary (B) and ternary (T) choice reflects a condition-unspecific change in behaviour, that is, an accuracy reduction potentially induced by higher cognitive demands in the ternary trials.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential confound that was considered.

claims.claim: This 'generic' bias was estimated by a permutation procedure whereby the true mappings between ternary conditions and their matched binary conditions were randomly shuffled and an average T − B accuracy contrast was obtained across random permutations.
claims.source: We estimated this 'generic' bias by a permutation procedure whereby we randomly shuffled the true mappings between ternary conditions and their matched binary conditions and obtained an average T − B accuracy contrast across random permutations (Figure 4c; see Methods).

claims.claim: The bias-corrected T − B relative accuracy change shows a strong attraction effect: The relative choice accuracy dynamically decreases and increases as an inferior D gets closer to L (n = 32 relevant trials) and H (n = 33), respectively, |t(143)| > 4.88, p < 0.0001.
claims.source: The bias-corrected T − B relative accuracy change shows a strong attraction effect: The relative choice accuracy dynamically decreases and increases as an inferior D gets closer to L (n = 32 relevant trials in this category) and H (n = 33), respectively, |t(143)| > 4.88, p < 0.0001 (Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing the attraction effect.

claims.claim: A significant repulsion effect occurs when a superior D dominates H or L in the attribute space, t(143) = −2.53, p = 0.025, particularly when D is closer to H (n = 41 relevant trials), but not when D is closer L (n = 20 relevant trials; t(143) = −1.09, p = 0.28, Bonferroni–Holm corrected).
claims.source: Meanwhile, a significant repulsion effect occurs when a superior D dominates H or L in the attribute space, t(143) = −2.53, p = 0.025, particularly when D is closer to H (n = 41 relevant trials in this category), but not when D is closer L (fewer trials n = 20 in this category; t(143) = −1.09, p = 0.28, Bonferroni–Holm corrected).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing the repulsion effect.

claims.claim: A repeated-measures ANOVA reveals a significant interaction between the similarity (D closer to H vs. D closer to L) and the dominance of D (inferior vs. superior), F(1, 143) = 30.6, p < 0.0001, partial η² = 0.18, on the T − B relative accuracy change.
claims.source: A repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) reveals a significant interaction between the similarity (D closer to H vs. D closer to L) and the dominance of D (inferior vs. superior), F(1, 143) = 30.6, p < 0.0001, partial η2 = 0.18, on the T − B relative accuracy change.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from an ANOVA.

claims.claim: In line with the AU-based negative distractor effect, the analysis on multiattribute decoy effects reveals a significant main effect of D's AU dominance on relative accuracy change, F(1, 143) = 6.51, p = 0.012, partial η² = 0.044.
claims.source: Of note, in line with the AU-based negative distractor effect we reported in the previous section, the current analysis on multiattribute decoy effects also reveals a significant main effect of D's AU dominance on relative accuracy change (repeated-measures ANOVA on T − B relative accuracy change in all trials), F(1, 143) = 6.51, p = 0.012, partial η2 = 0.044 (Figure 4f: 'Human').
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from an ANOVA.

claims.claim: The overall dominance effect seems to be induced by a noticeable asymmetry in the observed decoy effects: targeting H seems more effective than targeting L, and also, the attraction effect is stronger than the repulsion effect.
claims.source: This overall dominance effect seems to be induced by a noticeable asymmetry in the observed decoy effects (Figure 4d, net of inferior-purple vs. superior-blue bars): targeting H seems more effective than targeting L, and also, the attraction effect is stronger than the repulsion effect (hence, the multiattribute effects do not cancel out but lead to a net accuracy boost for inferior D's).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern of decoy effects.

claims.claim: Across participants there is a significant positive correlation between the negative main distractor effect 'AUD × C' and the negative main effect of D's AU dominance (Spearman's ρ = 0.28, p = 0.00074).
claims.source: Crucially, across participants there is a significant positive correlation between the negative main distractor effect 'AUD × C' (GLM in the previous section) and the negative main effect of D's AU dominance here (Spearman's ρ = 0.28, p = 0.00074).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing a correlation between two effects.

claims.claim: If a participant had a stronger asymmetry in the decoy effects (D's AU dominance) then they would also have a stronger AU-based negative distractor effect.
claims.source: This indicates that if a participant had a stronger asymmetry in the decoy effects (D's AU dominance) then they would also have a stronger AU-based negative distractor effect.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation result.

claims.claim: The AU model is essentially a context-independent model complying with the IIA principle.
claims.source: Although the AU model successfully described behavioural responses in binary trials (Figure 3), it is essentially a context-independent model complying with the independence from irrelevant alternatives (IIA) principle.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the AU model.

claims.claim: According to the AU model, the characteristics of D in ternary trials should not lead to any preference change between the two available targets H and L.
claims.source: That is, according to the AU model, the characteristics of D in ternary trials should not lead to any preference change between the two available targets H and L.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the AU model being context-independent.

claims.claim: The T − B effects in human data could not be explained by a context-independent AU model with freely varying parameters across B and T conditions.
claims.source: First, as shown in Figure 4e leftmost panel, the T − B effects in human data could not be explained by a context-independent AU model ('blind' to D, i.e., only taking H and L as inputs) with freely varying parameters across B and T conditions (the free parameters could capture any global changes in behaviour due to, for example, different noise levels and/or attribute weighting, potentially induced by higher cognitive demands in the ternary trials; Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: Two models that can predict context effects in multiattribute choice were considered: selective integration (SI) and adaptive gain.
claims.source: Next, we considered two models that can predict context effects in multiattribute choice: selective integration (SI) and adaptive gain (Dumbalska et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018; Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the models considered for explaining context effects.

claims.claim: In the SI model, the gain of processing on each attribute value relies on its rank within that attribute, with a selective gating parameter w controlling the suppression strength for the low-rank attribute value.
claims.source: In the SI model, the gain of processing on each attribute value relies on its rank within that attribute, with a selective gating parameter w controlling the suppression strength for the low-rank attribute value.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of the SI model.

claims.claim: In the adaptive gain model, each alternative is evaluated relative to the context statistics via a non-linear function.
claims.source: In the adaptive gain model, each alternative is evaluated relative to the context statistics via a non-linear function.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of the adaptive gain model.

claims.claim: The SI model can reproduce all types of attraction and repulsion effects in the data, but a dual-route model cannot.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4e, the SI model can reproduce all types of attraction and repulsion effects in the data, but a dual-route model cannot.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling comparing model predictions to human data.

claims.claim: A systematic Bayesian random-effects model comparison shows that SI prevails over all other models (Ppexc > 0.99).
claims.source: A systematic Bayesian random-effects model comparison shows that SI prevails over all other models (Ppexc > 0.99; Figure 4g), including the dual-route, DN, or any context-independent model with either EV or AU as the utility function (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian model comparison.

claims.claim: The adaptive gain model captures some key context effects, although not as closely as the SI model does.
claims.source: The adaptive gain model captures some key context effects, although not as closely as the SI model does (fixed-effects: SI vs. adaptive gain, cross-validated log-likelihood ratio = 219.8, ΔBIC = −1194, pooled over participants; random-effects: SI's Ppexc > 0.99; Figure 4e)
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling and model comparison.

claims.claim: The adaptive gain model explains the human data decisively better than the dual-route model.
claims.source: and explains the human data decisively better than the dual-route model (adaptive gain vs. dual-route: cross-validated log-likelihood ratio = 48.58, ΔBIC = −806, pooled over participants; adaptive gain's Ppexc = 0.78; see Supplementary file 4 for model parameters).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling and model comparison.

claims.claim: A model recovery procedure confirmed that the Bayesian model comparison was capable of properly discriminating among the context-dependent models (SI, adaptive gain, and dual-route).
claims.source: A model recovery procedure (Methods) also confirmed that our Bayesian model comparison was capable of properly discriminating among these context-dependent models (SI, adaptive gain, and dual-route; Figure 4h).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a model recovery analysis.

claims.claim: The SI model could lawfully reproduce the overall negative D's AU dominance effect without relying on any additional mechanism such as DN, F(1, 143) = 78.4, p < 0.00001, partial η² = 0.35, post hoc t-test: t(143) = −8.85, p < 0.0001.
claims.source: Crucially, the SI model could lawfully reproduce the overall negative D's AU dominance effect without relying on any additional mechanism such as DN, F(1, 143) = 78.4, p < 0.00001, partial η2 = 0.35, post hoc t-test: t(143) = −8.85, p < 0.0001 (Figure 4f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The models that predict 'by-design' unidimensional distractor effect (dual-route and DN) could not describe the multiattribute decoy effects.
claims.source: By contrast, the models that predict 'by-design' unidimensional distractor effect (dual-route and DN) could not describe the multiattribute decoy effects (Figure 4e, f; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The negative D dominance effect is not the by-product of a unidimensional distractor mechanism but instead falls out naturally from the presence of asymmetrical decoy effects.
claims.source: This suggests that the negative D dominance effect is not the by-product of a unidimensional distractor mechanism but instead falls out naturally from the presence of asymmetrical decoy effects (i.e., stronger attraction effect, when H is targeted).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claims.claim: The correlation between the D dominance and AU distractor effects corroborates the possibility that, to some extent, the negative distractor effect is driven by asymmetrical decoy effects.
claims.source: The correlation between the D dominance and AU distractor effects discussed above, corroborates the possibility that, to some extent, the negative distractor effect is driven by asymmetrical decoy effects (Figure 4f: SI model mimics the negative D dominance effect).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation linking the correlation to the modeling results.

claims.claim: Because SI selectively allocates reduced gain to 'locally losing' attribute values, it exerts a stronger gating on the utility of option B when the decoy D dominates B than when D is dominated by B.
claims.source: Because SI selectively allocates reduced gain to 'locally losing' attribute values, it exerts a stronger gating on the utility of option B when the decoy D dominates B (Figure 5b) than when D is dominated by B (Figure 5a).
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism by which SI produces context effects.

claims.claim: The relative preference between A and B can be dynamically reversed according to the dominance of D, giving rise to the opposing context effects of attraction and repulsion.
claims.source: Thus, the relative preference between A and B can be dynamically reversed according to the dominance of D, giving rise to the opposing context effects of attraction and repulsion.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the SI mechanism.

claims.claim: SI has been shown to maximise decision accuracy and economic outcomes in the face of decision noise that arises when multiple attributes or pieces of information need to be combined towards a decision.
claims.source: Lastly, SI has been shown to maximise decision accuracy and economic outcomes in the face of decision noise that arises when multiple attributes or pieces of information need to be combined towards a decision (Tsetsos et al., 2016; Wyart and Koechlin, 2016).
claims.evidence: This references previous work on the normative properties of SI, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A positive correlation was found across participants between the SI gating w and the temperature of a softmax choice function (Spearman's ρ(142) > 0.43, p < 0.0001, for both binary and ternary choices).
claims.source: After fitting a static version of the SI model to choice probabilities (Methods), we found a positive correlation across participants between the SI gating w and the temperature of a softmax choice function (Spearman's ρ(142) > 0.43, p < 0.0001, for both binary and ternary choices; Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claims.claim: Additional parameter-recovery simulations corroborated that the findings about the correlation between SI w and decision noise are not due to any trade-off between model parameters.
claims.source: Additional parameter-recovery simulations corroborated that these findings are not due to any trade-off between model parameters (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter recovery simulations.

claims.claim: After fitting the dynamic SI model to choices and RTs together, the SI w negatively correlates with the utility drift sensitivity (how effective a participant is in using the information about utility), but not the height of the decision bound.
claims.source: After fitting the dynamic SI model to choices and RTs together, we found that the SI w negatively correlates with the utility drift sensitivity (how effective a participant is in using the information about utility; Methods), but not the height of the decision bound (Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claims.claim: The findings suggest that SI has an adaptive role, as it selectively exaggerates the attribute difference between winning and losing alternatives by just the right amount in proportion to decision noise.
claims.source: These findings suggest that SI has an adaptive role, as it selectively exaggerates the attribute difference between winning and losing alternatives by just the right amount in proportion to decision noise.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claims.claim: The findings clarify the modulatory role of an unavailable distracting option, shedding fresh light on the mechanisms that govern multiattribute decisions.
claims.source: These findings clarify the modulatory role of an unavailable distracting option, shedding fresh light on the mechanisms that govern multiattribute decisions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claims.claim: The previously reported positive and interacting effects can be explained away by confounding covariations among distractor variables and subjective utility, which in these datasets was shaped by additive and not multiplicative reward/probability integration.
claims.source: We found that the previously reported positive and interacting effects can be explained away by confounding covariations among distractor variables and subjective utility, which in these datasets was shaped by additive and not multiplicative reward/probability integration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claims.claim: The multiattribute context effects occurring here were technically 'phantom' effects due to the fact that the distractor could not be chosen.
claims.source: Of note, the multiattribute context effects occurring here were technically 'phantom' effects (Pettibone and Wedell, 2007) due to the fact that the distractor could not be chosen
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the context effects observed, with a citation.

claims.claim: Contrary to most previous demonstrations, where the target and competitor alternatives are almost equally valuable, the effects reported here arise even under a noticeable value difference between the target and the competitor.
claims.source: and contrary to most previous demonstrations, where the target and competitor alternatives are almost equally valuable, the effects we reported here arise even under a noticeable value difference between the target and the competitor (Farmer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous work, with a citation.

claims.claim: The context effects were asymmetric in magnitude, yielding an average accuracy increase for inferior distractors and an average accuracy decrease for superior ones, mirroring the negative distractor effect.
claims.source: These context effects were asymmetric in magnitude, yielding an average accuracy increase for inferior distractors and an average accuracy decrease for superior ones, mirroring thus the negative distractor effect.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claims.claim: The negative distractor effect reported is of rather small size.
claims.source: Notably, the negative distractor effect we reported is of rather small size.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the magnitude of the effect.

claims.claim: A plausible explanation of the negative distractor effect is that it could be driven, to some extent, by asymmetric multiattribute context effects.
claims.source: A plausible explanation of this negative distractor effect is that it could be driven, to some extent, by asymmetric multiattribute context effects.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation offered by the authors.

claims.claim: From an empirical perspective, the 'dominance' effect arising from multiattribute decoy effects correlates with the negative distractor effect.
claims.source: We made this conjecture for two reasons. First, from an empirical perspective, the 'dominance' effect arising from multiattribute decoy effects correlates with the negative distractor effect.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of an empirical finding.

claims.claim: From a theoretical perspective, model comparison favours by large a model that can only produce multiattribute decoy effects and has no dedicated mechanism to generate unidimensional distractor effects.
claims.source: Second, from a theoretical perspective, model comparison favours by large a model that can only produce multiattribute decoy effects and has no dedicated mechanism to generate unidimensional distractor effects.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a modeling finding.

claims.claim: The link between the distractor and decoy effects is interpreted with caution given that there are differences in the way the two effects were quantified.
claims.source: However, we interpret the link between the distractor and decoy effects with caution given that there are differences in the way the two effects were quantified.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary note about the interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: In the distractor effect, the key variable is defined continuously (i.e., the distractor's utility) while in decoy effects, 'dominance' is defined categorically (superior or inferior to the target).
claims.source: In the distractor effect, the key variable is defined continuously (i.e., the distractor's utility) while in decoy effects, 'dominance' is defined categorically (superior or inferior to the target).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological difference in how the two effects were quantified.

claims.claim: A less parsimonious hybrid model in which both unidimensional distractor mechanism (i.e., DN) and multiattribute context sensitivities (i.e., SI) coexist has not been ruled out.
claims.source: Similarly, a less parsimonious hybrid model in which both unidimensional distractor mechanism (i.e., DN) and multiattribute context sensitivities (i.e., SI) coexist has not been ruled out.
claims.evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claims.claim: Definitive conclusions on the link between distractor and decoy effects await new experimental designs in which the two types of effects can be quantified independently.
claims.source: Definitive conclusions on the link between distractor and decoy effects await new experimental designs in which the two types of effects can be quantified independently.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claims.claim: In light of the stronger robust presence of decoy effects in these datasets, the hypothesis that multiattribute complexity is a key moderator of context dependencies, remains viable.
claims.source: In light of the stronger robust presence of decoy effects in these datasets, the hypothesis that multiattribute complexity is a key moderator of context dependencies, remains viable (Hunt et al., 2014; Juechems and Summerfield, 2019; Fellows, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to a broader hypothesis, with citations.

claims.claim: Encoding absolute information along several attributes is inefficient and suffers from the curse of dimensionality.
claims.source: Encoding absolute information along several attributes is inefficient (Summerfield and Tsetsos, 2015) and suffers from the curse of dimensionality (Sutton, 1988; Bellman, 1957).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about computational principles, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A plausible solution to circumvent the issues of encoding absolute information along several attributes is to discard information that is less important.
claims.source: A plausible solution to circumvent these issues is to discard information that is less important (Niv, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The SI model preferentially focuses on larger values at the expense of smaller values, and because of this policy, context effects ensue.
claims.source: In a similar spirit, our SI model preferentially focuses on larger values at the expense of smaller values, and because of this policy, context effects ensue.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of the SI model.

claims.claim: This selective policy potentially maximises robustness to decision noise, providing a normative justification of contextual preference reversal.
claims.source: This selective policy potentially maximises robustness to decision noise (Tsetsos et al., 2016; Luyckx et al., 2020), providing thus a normative justification of contextual preference reversal.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the SI model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Although the SI model had thus far been applied to dynamic (sequential) value accumulation tasks, it can also account for behaviour in a static multiattribute task.
claims.source: And although the SI model had thus far been applied to dynamic (sequential) value accumulation tasks (Usher et al., 2019), we here show that it can also account for behaviour in a static multiattribute task.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a contribution of the current study, with a citation.

claims.claim: SI, despite its simplicity and computational tractability, is not claimed to be the only computational model that could explain the multiattribute context effects in this task.
claims.source: Nevertheless, we do not claim that SI, despite its simplicity and computational tractability, is the only computational model that could explain the multiattribute context effects in this task (Noguchi and Stewart, 2018; Trueblood et al., 2014; Bhatia, 2013; Roe et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary note acknowledging alternative models, with citations.

claims.claim: Contrary to the normative rule, participants in the datasets analysed integrated probability and payoff information additively and not multiplicatively.
claims.source: Notably, and contrary to the normative rule, participants in the datasets we analysed integrated probability and payoff information additively and not multiplicatively.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claims.claim: This additive integration, or more generally, the processing of information in a 'within dimensions' fashion, is probably what spurs contextual preference reversal in risky choice.
claims.source: This additive integration, or more generally, the processing of information in a 'within dimensions' fashion, is probably what spurs contextual preference reversal in risky choice.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: A large and influential body of research in risky decision-making supports the idea that non-linear transformations of probabilities and rewards are multiplicatively combined (e.g., prospect theory).
claims.source: However, unlike what we observed here, a large and influential body of research in risky decision-making supports the idea that non-linear transformations of probabilities and rewards are multiplicatively combined (e.g., prospect theory, Kahneman and Tversky, 1979).
claims.evidence: This references a large body of previous research, with a citation.

claims.claim: Additive integration in risky choice has limited applicability as opposed to the more widely applied multiplicative-integration framework.
claims.source: Additive integration in risky choice has limited applicability as opposed to the more widely applied multiplicative-integration framework.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the scope of applicability of additive integration.

claims.claim: Unlike multiplicative models, the additive-integration framework enforces independent contributions of reward and probability and cannot readily accommodate rich attitudes towards risk or other complex phenomena in decisions over multibranch gambles.
claims.source: Unlike multiplicative models, the additive-integration framework enforces independent contributions of reward and probability (Koechlin, 2020) and cannot readily accommodate rich attitudes towards risk (Tversky and Wakker, 1995) or other complex phenomena in decisions over multibranch gambles (Birnbaum, 2006; Birnbaum, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of additive integration, supported by citations.

claims.claim: At a fundamental level, additive integration requires ad hoc assumptions to capture the decreasing desirability of negative outcomes with increasing probability, or risk-attitudes over mixed gambles that offer both positive and negative outcomes.
claims.source: At an even more fundamental level, additive integration requires ad hoc assumptions (on the way outcomes and probabilities are represented) to capture the decreasing desirability of negative outcomes with increasing probability, or risk-attitudes over mixed gambles that offer both positive and negative outcomes (Tom et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of additive integration, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Although these limitations suggest that additive integration is not readily generalisable to all types of risky choice, this does not undermine its descriptive superiority in simpler tasks like the one focused on here.
claims.source: Although these limitations suggest that additive integration is not readily generalisable to all types of risky choice, this does not undermine its descriptive superiority in simpler tasks like the one we focused on here.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the scope of the findings.

claims.claim: One overarching conjecture is that the stimulus employed in different experiments determines the way participants integrate reward and probability, with multiplicative integration observed in numerically explicit gambles and additive integration when rewards and probabilities are inferred from abstract non-numerical (perceptual) dimensions.
claims.source: One overarching conjecture is that the stimulus employed in different experiments determines the way participants integrate reward and probability, with multiplicative integration observed in numerically explicit gambles and additive integration when rewards and probabilities are inferred from abstract non-numerical (perceptual) dimensions (Rouault et al., 2019; Stewart, 2011; Farashahi et al., 2019; Bongioanni et al., 2021; Koechlin, 2020; Massi et al., 2018; Donahue and Lee, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conjecture about the factors that determine integration strategy, supported by citations.

claims.claim: This may further suggest that risk preference is a rather elusive and unstable construct.
claims.source: This may further suggest that risk preference is a rather elusive and unstable construct (Chater et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Additive and multiplicative integration strategies are not necessarily mutually exclusive, and they could instead co-influence risky decisions.
claims.source: Additive and multiplicative integration strategies are not necessarily mutually exclusive, and they could instead co-influence risky decisions (Farashahi et al., 2019; Bongioanni et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the potential coexistence of integration strategies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Neural correlates of both additive and multiplicative decision variables have been reported within the same task and even within overlapping brain regions.
claims.source: More generally, neural correlates of both additive and multiplicative decision variables have been reported within the same task and even within overlapping brain regions.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about neuroscience findings.

claims.claim: Neural signals in a network of cortical and subcortical brain regions have been shown to code for value/utility-related metrics of diverse assets.
claims.source: Neural signals in a network of cortical and subcortical brain regions have been shown to code for value/utility-related metrics of diverse assets (Tom et al., 2007; De Martino et al., 2006; Platt and Glimcher, 1999; Kennerley et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about neuroscience findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Within the value-coding network, the dorsal medial frontal cortex (dmPFC) seems to be particularly relevant for the multiplicative integration of reward and probability in risky decisions.
claims.source: Within this network, the dorsal medial frontal cortex (dmPFC in humans [Hunt et al., 2014] and an anterior/dorsal frontal site located between the rostral and anterior cingulate sulci in area 32 of non-human primates [Bongioanni et al., 2021]) seems to be particularly relevant for the multiplicative integration of reward and probability in risky decisions.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about neuroscience findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A focal ultrasonic disruption of the anterior/dorsal frontal region (but not the posterior/ventral medial frontal cortex [vmPFC]) caused a shift from a multiplicative to an additive strategy in macaques.
claims.source: Strikingly, a focal ultrasonic disruption of this anterior/dorsal frontal region (but not the posterior/ventral medial frontal cortex [vmPFC]) caused a shift from a multiplicative to an additive strategy in the macaques (Bongioanni et al., 2021), imputing a direct causal link between EV computation and the dorsal medial frontal lobe.
